1:
When the invasion happened is argued from a reading that may not belong to the text. Gill accepts it, dating the siege a month after Saul was chosen on the authority of the Greek and Latin versions and of Josephus. Clarke reports the same addition but rejects it: wanting in the Complutensian edition in both languages, probably inserted into some Greek copies from Josephus and thence into the Latin, and so of very little authority. Keil and Delitzsch separate the two questions: the Hebrew gives no date, but a later chapter makes it evident that Nahash had invaded Gilead before the election, while the emendation behind the Greek reading, which Ewald and Thenius would adopt, is unsupported by every other ancient version. Wesley leaves it open, allowing either that the invasion preceded and prompted the demand for a king, or that only Nahash's preparations did.

The grievance is the old one. Keil and Delitzsch have Nahash enforcing his ancestor's claim to part of Gilead from Jephthah's day, and Ellicott makes it revenge for Jephthah's slaughter, the moment judged favourable because Samuel was now old. Clarke, noting a king of the same name in David's time, thinks it probably a different man and the name perhaps common to Ammonite kings. Why the city offered to capitulate draws four different answers. Clarke says simply that they were in no condition to risk a war. Ellicott puts it down to their isolation and distance from the centre of the nation, and Wesley to their seeing no likelihood of relief from their brethren in Canaan. Henry lays it to apostasy, since they had lost the virtue of Israelites and so the valour of them, and need not have courted a covenant with a Gentile nation had they kept their covenant with God.

The condition Nahash set is explained by the same military fact in three places. Clarke quotes Theodoret, that a man holding his shield in his left hand hides his left eye and looks at the enemy with his right, so that plucking out the right eye makes him useless in war, and notes that Josephus gives the same reason; Ellicott and Henry say the same. Henry adds the exquisite pain of it and the reproach it would fix on an Israel that let one of its chief cities be so used. Wesley notices what is left as much as what is taken: one eye remains, so that the men may still serve in any mean and base office. Keil and Delitzsch settle the grammar, that it is Nahash and not the Israelites who does the thrusting out, against two of the versions, and that the reproach refers to the blinding itself.

Whether the besieged knew they had a king divides the voices evenly. Keil and Delitzsch infer from the embassy to all Israel that there was no central government and that neither Nahash nor the Jabeshites had heard of the election; Clarke argues the same from the message being addressed to the people and not to Saul. Gill and Ellicott hold the opposite, that the messengers came to Gibeah directly because they knew the chosen king lived there, the respite being asked, Ellicott adds, in hope of Saul himself, in whose election they had lately taken part. Behind that lies a tie three of them explain. Ellicott tells it fully: Jabesh alone refused the summons against Gibeah, was razed for it, and its spared maidens were afterwards given to the remnant of Benjamin; Gill makes the point from the Benjamite side, Henry from the city's, replenished by the posterity of those who escaped that sword and in danger again as though some fate attended the place. On the weeping Clarke and Ellicott agree that they saw no way to help, and Henry puts it sharply, that they would sooner shed tears for their brethren than blood.
5:
That the elected king was still following the cattle is explained four ways. Gill makes it necessity: chosen but not inaugurated, taking no state, despised by some, with no provision settled for his support and no business while Samuel still acted in his office, he went back to his father's rustic work. Ellicott makes it policy: the royal authority was new in a republican Israel, its duties vague, and the jealousies already noticed would have induced Saul to keep the kingship in the background. Henry makes it humility: Saul did not think it beneath him to know the state of his own flocks, and was unwilling to burden a people who had settled no revenue on him. Clarke makes it a providential interval, then quietly dismantles the moral others draw from it: men remark that great kings and generals have been taken from the plough, but forget that in ancient times agriculture was the only employment, so that every dignity had to be filled from that class.

What came upon him next is read along a scale. Gill has the Spirit fill him with pity for the men of Jabesh, with wisdom to contrive their relief and with fortitude to attempt it, and cites the Targum for a spirit of fortitude resting on him. Ellicott has the Spirit fall on a heart already moved by the peril of his tribe's old ally, enduing him with wisdom, valour and power as it had the judges. Keil and Delitzsch refer the kindled anger to the shame the Ammonites meant to fix on all Israel. Clarke will allow much less, holding that the words mean no more than that his courage was greatly excited and he felt strong for the fight. Henry goes furthest the other way and itemises the anger: at the insolence of the Ammonites, at the sneaking spirit of the men of Jabesh, at their not having sent word sooner, and at neighbours weeping when it was fitter to be arming.

The summons by hewn oxen is matched with parallels from three places. Keil and Delitzsch set it beside the cutting up of the woman in Judges and say the act made a deep impression; Clarke makes the same comparison and adds the bloody cross sent round to call the Highland clans to battle. Ellicott quotes Ewald for the war-arrow passed on in Norway and the fire-brand dipped in blood at both ends sent round in Scotland,. Wesley gives the reason behind the method, that the sight of men's eyes affects their hearts much more than what they only hear. Henry attends to the threat attached and finds it mild: not thus shall it be done to the man, but thus to his oxen, and far short of the penalty the whole congregation had once set for the same refusal, Saul wishing to show his government gentler than what they had known.

Why Samuel's name stands beside his own is given three accounts. Keil and Delitzsch take it as proof that Saul as king still recognised the prophet's authority. Wesley has him joined because he was present and because his name added weight, and Henry calls it modesty. On what then fell upon the people Keil and Delitzsch are careful: the fear of Jehovah is not to be read as the panic terror Thenius and Böttcher make it. Wesley takes it as a fear sent by God so that none dared refuse help, and draws from it that the fear of God makes men good subjects and good soldiers. Ellicott turns it into an argument from history, finding the same awakening behind the psalmist's image of the Lord rousing as one out of sleep, and behind the Swiss at Laupen and Morat and the traders of Holland who drove out the armies of Spain.
8:
Where the muster was held is agreed, but not quite what the word means. Keil and Delitzsch place Bezek by the old gazetteer about seven hours north of Nabulus towards Beisan, and Ellicott puts it in Issachar in the plain of Jezreel, open country well suited to assembling a great host at short notice. Gill accepts the place but records an alternative that makes the word a common noun rather than a name: it may mean with a stone, each man bringing one to be laid on a heap and the heap then counted, the Greek word for little stones being adduced for it, or with a fragment, a potsherd or a broken stone or a branch carried in the hand, so that the king's servants counted not men but tokens.

The numbers themselves are defended, doubted and qualified in turn. Keil and Delitzsch see no difficulty, since this was not a regular army but a general levy of the whole people. Clarke doubts the whole tradition: the Greek raises the figures to six hundred thousand and seventy thousand and Josephus higher still, these cannot all be right, and he suspects the Hebrew itself of exaggeration by the mistake or the design of some ancient scribe. Ellicott takes a middle line, rejecting the suggestion that the verse is a late reviser's insertion while allowing that in these books numbers are not always to be relied upon through copyists' errors. Why Judah is counted apart then divides them sharply. Keil and Delitzsch find in it an early trace of the separation that ended in formal secession, and Ellicott hears an undertone of sadness that the rich and populous southern tribe contributed only thirty thousand, quoting Dean Payne Smith that Judah always stood apart until it had a king of its own. Wesley reads the same figure as a credit: they are numbered apart to their honour, since the tribe to whom the kingdom was promised submitted readily to a king of another tribe, and hazarded themselves for their brethren when they might have pleaded the defence of their own border against the Philistines.

On the promise sent back, Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott agree that help by the time the sun was hot means about noon, Ellicott adding that the distance to be covered was not much over twenty miles. The answer the besieged then returned to Nahash is judged differently. Keil and Delitzsch call it an untruth, told to make the besiegers secure so that Saul's advance might fall on them unawares; Clarke puts it as concealment rather than falsehood, and notes grimly that they did come out to the Ammonites, though not in the manner expected. The attack is closely timed. Clarke supposes the march began in the evening, crossed Jordan by night and reached the camp by daybreak, and takes the three companies as meant to strike at three points and give the men room to act, which Keil and Delitzsch describe as forcing their way in from three sides. On the hour they differ a little, Keil and Delitzsch putting the morning watch between three and six and Ellicott between two and six, he explaining it as the last of three watches of four hours each in the old Hebrew reckoning, and reckoning that the rout went on for many hours. Both read the closing detail the same way: that no two were left together proves the rout complete.
12:
That the people address Samuel and not the king raises a question about where Samuel was, and two voices answer it the same way. Gill infers that he had accompanied the expedition, finds it hard that a man of his years should have kept up with so quick a march, and settles on his having followed gently and met them soon after the battle; Henry reaches the same conclusion independently, that Samuel was present to meet them on their return if not in the action, the march being too far for him. Henry adds why the motion went to him rather than to Saul: they knew Saul would not be judge in his own cause. Ellicott takes the same fact as a measure of the seer's standing, that even in the first flush of the new king's victory it was to Samuel the people looked for the punishment of those who had questioned the election, and he recalls that the summons itself had run in both their names. Keil and Delitzsch settle the form of the words, which are a question carried by tone alone and need no alteration of the text to make them one, and refer them back to the worthless men of the previous chapter.

What moved the demand is read unkindly by both voices that take it up. Clarke has them flushed with victory and proud of their leader, wanting to prove their attachment by killing in cool blood the men who had at first been averse to him, and generalises without mercy: the common soldier is scarcely ever inspired by a victory to acts of magnanimity, having shed blood he wishes to shed more. Henry makes the same point from the other side, that Saul's success did more to confirm his title with them than either the lot or Samuel's anointing, and that they had wanted the courage to prosecute his opponents while he looked mean, but now that victory made him look great nothing would serve but putting them to death.

The answer is praised by everyone and explained five ways. Clarke sets it simply against the soldiers' proposal, as much to Saul's credit as that was to their discredit. Keil and Delitzsch find in it not only magnanimity but genuine piety. Ellicott calls it wise as well as generous, since a bloody vengeance would have begun lasting feuds with the powerful families who had opposed the election, and holds that Saul taught kings to come how truly royal a virtue forgiveness is, his heart being as yet unspoiled; the reasoning he quotes for it, that God's own clemency that day left them bound to forgive without bloodshed, he takes from Schmidt by way of Keil and Delitzsch. Henry gives two reasons, that the day was one of joy and triumph and ought not to be made harsh, and that an enemy reclaimed is more to our advantage than an enemy slain, since all good princes know their power is for edification and not destruction. Gill alone keeps one eye on what came later: the pardon was lenity and also policy at the opening of a reign, and it plainly appears that this temper did not always continue with him.
14:
Why the assembly was called when it was, and where, is answered by three voices in agreement. Gill has Samuel fall in with Saul's pardon and propose the journey partly to turn the people off their demand for the offenders' lives, and partly to take them while their temper was good. Wesley reads the same timing as prudence and fidelity together: Samuel had suspended the confirmation while the generality were disaffected, and now that Saul had given eminent proof of his princely virtues and the people's hearts were set on him, he judged this the fittest season. Ellicott recalls how much there had been to repair, the original election at Mizpeh having met with murmurings and no unanimous acceptance of the Benjamite now crowned with a splendid success, and he marks the generosity of a seer who presented to Israel again the man who had superseded him as judge. On the place he notes the well-known sanctuary in the Jordan valley not far from Jericho, scene of much of the nation's history, chosen no doubt because it lay in what was now the royal tribe.

Whether Saul was anointed a second time there is the chapter's open question, and the two voices that address it divide. Clarke holds it likely from the words themselves, on the ground that the first unction had been a very private act and the appointment not generally known, where Saul had now shown himself worthy to command and there was no gainsayer; and he reports that Josephus says plainly that Saul was anointed again at this convocation. Ellicott refuses it: we must not understand with the Greek version, which reads that Samuel anointed Saul king there, that any fresh anointing took place, the Gilgal convention being nothing more than a solemn national confirmation of the popular election at Mizpeh. What the phrase before the Lord implies he takes to be the presence of the ark, or of the high priest with the Urim and Thummim; and for the sense of making Saul king he quotes Bishop Wordsworth, that from this time the people would no longer allow him to lead a private life but made him assume the state and authority to which God had appointed him.

Clarke closes the chapter with material that belongs to its opening. At this last verse he prints a long letter from a correspondent on the hewn oxen, arguing first that the authenticity of a people's records is well illustrated by customs resembling those of other nations at a similar stage, and the more so when the resemblance is not close enough to suggest copying. The comparison offered is the Highland fiery cross, with Scott's description of the rites that preceded its circulation, and the Scandinavian practice recorded by Olaus Magnus of punishing disobedience to the summons with death and the burning of houses: with the Highlanders a goat was killed and a blood-stained cross carried round, with Israel an ox, and part of the animal itself was the mandate, the penalty being not death but the forfeiture of the beasts. The same letter adds a military reason for the condition Nahash set, since the right eye is what chiefly aids a man in aiming his weapon, which makes the mutilation less purely wanton than revenge would have made it. Clarke's own last word looks forward rather than back: so far Saul had acted well and the kingdom seemed confirmed in his hand, but through imprudence he soon lost it.
